node.label: Patricia Crone
node.date_label: Hagarism (1977, with Michael Cook) · Slaves on Horses (1980) · God’s Caliph (1986, with Martin Hinds) · Pre-Industrial Societies (1989) · Medieval Islamic Political Thought / God’s Rule (2004) · The Nativist Prophets (2012)
node.description: Patricia Crone challenged the use of later Muslim narratives as straightforward evidence for Islam’s beginnings. In Hagarism: The Making of the Islamic World (1977), written with Michael Cook, she proposed a radical rewriting of early Islamic history. R. Stephen Humphreys credited the book with forcing historians to reconsider their sources while observing that very few accepted its reconstruction. Crone’s subsequent work examined the relations between tribal society, religious authority and imperial government. Yahya Sadowski criticized her account of enduring tribal biases in Islam as essentialist. God’s Rule, also published as Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004), traces competing political arguments across six centuries; Guillaume Dye praised its connection of texts to social practices while flagging its reliance on the disputed thesis of God’s Caliph (1986, with Martin Hinds). Peter Brown welcomed The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012) for bringing Iran into late-antique religious history.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Hagarism (1977), with Michael Cook; Slaves on Horses (1980); God’s Caliph (1986), with Martin Hinds; Roman, Provincial and Islamic Law (1987); Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987); Pre-Industrial Societies (1989); Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004), published in the United States as God’s Rule; The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012).
node.scope_note: Selected primary passages of the revised Tribe and State chapter and the 2006 Post-Colonialism article were read. Major monographs were not read in full. Their arguments and reception are limited to the named reviews and institutional accounts. The Weber critique is mediated through Manzano; its German and English versions remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Eduardo Manzano notes (2015), Crone’s essay “Weber, Islamic Law, and the Rise of Capitalism” (revised English version 1999) criticizes Weber’s concept of rationality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Manzano, Medieval Worlds 1 (2015), p. 123 n. 22 (PDF page 6), explicitly identifies “A critique of Weber’s concept of rationality” in Crone’s essay, p. 251. Bibliography p. 135 gives the 1999 essay, pp. 247–272. Crone’s institutional bibliography distinguishes the 1987 German original from the revised English version. This is a named scholarly reader’s attribution; neither version of Crone’s essay nor Weber’s relevant original passage was read here, and their detailed positions are not reconstructed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Recovering Submerged Worlds (2013), Brown praises The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012) for bringing Iran into the history of late-antique religious and intellectual change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Brown’s review, paragraphs beginning For another side of the story and By doing this, followed by the final two paragraphs: praises bringing Iran into the “mainstream of late antique history” and commends following Crone’s and Bowersock’s example. Review body read; Crone’s book and the other reviewed books unread. Brown’s treatment is not presented as unqualified assent to every reconstruction.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pre-Industrial Societies (1989) takes a broad comparative approach to the common features of pre-industrial societies. It ranges from the Mongol Empire and the Ming dynasty to seventeenth-century France, draws parallels between imperial structures, and examines economic organization, politics, culture and religion, as the publisher’s description and Judith Herrin’s account (2015) state.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Original Preface in licensed 2015 Oneworld preview, paragraphs 1–5, and opening of chapter 1: explains constraints, uniformities and the distinction between common preindustrial features and civilization-specific ones. The author calls it a “rough-and-ready guide,” not a stringent ideal type. Preface and opening only; the main comparative chapters remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Guillaume Dye’s reading, God’s Rule / Medieval Islamic Political Thought (2004) explains competing political arguments through the changing social and political settings of Islamic texts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dye review, paragraphs beginning One of the main strengths and This may give the impression, then the sections on rightly guided rule and communal solidarity: stresses the relation between texts and practices and the plurality of positions within Islam. Whole review read; 2004 book unread. This connects to the broad intellectual-history field and does not infer membership in the Cambridge School.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Sadowski’s account, Slaves on Horses (1980) explains unstable political authority through the tension between tribal religious ideals and settled imperial government.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sadowski, Strong Society, Weak State, first three paragraphs, and endnotes 35–38, explicitly discuss Crone and cite Slaves on Horses pp. 62–63 and 84. His subsequent slave-soldier and modern-democracy claims also discuss Daniel Pipes and John Hall; those claims are not all assigned to Crone. Strong Society or Strong State?, first two substantive paragraphs, criticizes Crone’s persistence of tribal bias as essentialism. Named reader route; the book remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam (1987) challenged the accepted picture of Mecca as a major trading centre. In Judith Herrin’s summary, Crone argued that the spice trade was an Orientalist invention and that the trade depicted in the Muslim sources could not account for the supposed wealth and power of Quraysh.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Two institutional or memorial texts, both read in full. (1) Judith Herrin’s memoir, the introduction to the Festschrift Islamic Cultures, Islamic Contexts (Brill, 2015), pp. xiv–xx, republished on openDemocracy (12 July 2015, CC BY-NC). I read it in a 2017 Wayback capture of the openly published page; the live page now shows only the opening to readers who are not signed in. Paragraph beginning “In 1977 Patricia took up an appointment at Oxford”: “This was followed by Meccan Trade …”, “She argued that the spice trade was an Orientalist invention and that the trade depicted in the Muslim sources couldn’t account for the supposed wealth and power of Quraysh.” (2) The Institute for Advanced Study obituary (15 July 2015), read in a 2022 Wayback capture because ias.edu returned 403. Its paragraph beginning “This was followed by work that closely related to her doctoral thesis” says Meccan Trade “challenged the widely accepted understanding of Mecca as a major trade center”. Meccan Trade itself was not read. The claim is limited to these two characterisations of its argument. No claim is made about its reception among economic historians.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Getting the Conceptual Handles” (Government and Opposition, 1989), her review of Gellner’s Plough, Sword and Book (1988), Crone summarises his three-stage account of human history (hunter-gathering, agricultural and industrial) and his thesis that modern thought separates normative from referential truth. She notes that he writes at a high level of abstraction with few concrete examples, adds that informed readers will enjoy his concision, and judges that the overall vision makes compelling reading.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read on the publisher’s own page (Cambridge Core), which shows a first-page preview image of p. 375 because the item has no abstract. Government and Opposition 24:3 (1989), 375–378. Under the heading “Patricia Crone: Getting the Conceptual Handles. E. Gellner: Plough, Sword and Book. The Structure of Human History, London, Collins Harvill, 1988”, the paragraph beginning “The aim of this ambitiously, but not inappropriately, named book” sets out the stages (“hunter-gathering, agricultural and industrial”) and the book’s triad of cognition, political organization and production. It continues: “the author writes on a high level of abstraction with little in the way of concrete illustrations or examples, so that novices are likely soon to lose sight of what he is talking about”, and “Many of the arguments are familiar from his earlier works, but some are new and the overall vision makes compelling reading.” The next paragraph begins “The thesis may be summarized as follows. There are two kinds of truth, normative and referential.” Pp. 376–378 are unread, including any substantive disagreement. The critique claim is therefore limited to her stated reservation about abstraction, set beside her praise. If the coordinator prefers the Brown -> Crone review precedent (crone_w_03), it may be reclassified as connection/contribution.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Understanding Early Civilizations (2003), Trigger challenges the claim in Crone’s Pre-Industrial Societies (1989) that preindustrial societies lacked classes: Roman orders based on personal wealth, he argues, were classes even under her narrow definition. He nevertheless accepts the significance of her terminological distinction and of farmers’ difficulty in organizing collective action.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the primary text in the licensed Pageplace preview of Cambridge University Press’s Understanding Early Civilizations, chapter 3, printed pp. 45–46 (PDF pages 63–64 of 78). On p. 45 Trigger identifies Crone’s 1989 discussion at pp. 101–102, explains her distinction between strata and politically organized classes, and then uses Roman orders based on personal wealth as a counterexample. His concluding sentence on that page is the supporting_phrase below. The opening paragraph of p. 46 qualifies this disagreement by accepting the importance of her terminological concern and farmers’ organizational difficulties. The following paragraph explains his decision to retain class as a comparative category. Only this scholarly argument is used. Crone’s book itself was not read in this pass; its position is attributed to Trigger’s reading. The publisher’s chapter page confirms the original 2003 publication year and chapter range, pp. 40–52; its 2014 online date is not the work’s original year. The graph and supplied usable edges contain no Trigger–Crone relationship.
proposed_edges.map_label: Challenges restriction of class to industrial societies

proposed_edges.relationship: According to R. Stephen Humphreys, Crone and Michael Cook’s Hagarism: The Making of the Islamic World (1977) prompted historians of early Islam to re-examine their sources and methods, although very few accepted its reconstruction.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the institutional research-event report’s Hagarism assessment. This is reception evidence; the book remains unread. The target denotes source criticism broadly, without asserting Ranke transmission. Cook’s joint credit and limited acceptance are retained. The passage gives 1977, despite an inconsistent later reference to 1976.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chris Hann’s The Anthropology of Eurasia in Eurasia (2003) uses Crone’s Pre-Industrial Societies (1989; citing the 2003 edition) to advocate restoring broad historical comparison to anthropology beyond detailed local case studies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the institutional working paper, pp. 7–9 and bibliography p. 17. The claim concerns Hann’s documented use, not general adoption. Crone’s complete book remains unread; Hann cites its 2003 edition.
